HttpApi.reason: Keycloak's paths keep existing applications working; hashing and random tokens stay at the edge, as the idea's Not modelled says.

content.statement: The HTTP API serves Keycloak's token, introspection and logout endpoints for each realm, and lets an administrator enable or disable a user; it hashes the password with the user's salt and draws each token from a secure random source before calling the wiring.
content.why: Applications already speak Keycloak's OpenID Connect endpoints, so the paths and answers are Keycloak's. Hashing and drawing tokens happen here, outside the proven core (Not modelled): a 256-bit random token is distinct from every open one in practice, and the core refuses one that is not.

  "The HTTP API serves Keycloak's token, introspection and logout endpoints for each realm, and lets an administrator enable or disable a user; it hashes the password with the user's salt and draws each token from a secure random source before calling the wiring.",
  why = "Applications already speak Keycloak's OpenID Connect endpoints, so the paths and answers are Keycloak's. Hashing and drawing tokens happen here, outside the proven core (Not modelled): a 256-bit random token is distinct from every open one in practice, and the core refuses one that is not."
)("src/main/scala/keycloak/Server.scala")

content.statement: An introspection answers with the token's user and their roles exactly when the token's session is open in the realm asking and the user is enabled there; the claims name that realm.
content.why: ReferenceTokens for one request, as Keycloak's introspection endpoint answers it: the claims carry the user's realm roles, which applications use to authorise. abs: the user an answer names.

val introspectContract = referenceTokens.contractVia[RealmId, String, Option[Claims]](
  "Introspect",
  "An introspection answers with the token's user and their roles exactly when the token's session is open in the realm asking and the user is enabled there; the claims name that realm.",
  why = "ReferenceTokens for one request, as Keycloak's introspection endpoint answers it: the claims carry the user's realm roles, which applications use to authorise. abs: the user an answer names."
)(abs = f => (r, t) => claimedUser(f(r, t)))((realm, token, res) =>
  res.forall(c => c.realm == realm && sessionsByToken(token).exists(s => s.realm == realm && s.user == c.user) &&
    users.value.exists(a => a.realm == realm && a.username == c.user && a.enabled && a.roles == c.roles)) &&
  sessionsByToken(token).forall(s => (s.realm == realm && isEnabled(realm, s.user)) ==> res.isDefined))
  .examples(
    users.bind(List(UserAccount(RealmId("acme"), "alice", "h-alice", true, List("admin", "user")), UserAccount(RealmId("acme"), "bob", "h-bob", false, List("user")))),
    sessionsByToken.bindTable(Map("t1" -> Session("t1", RealmId("acme"), "alice"), "t2" -> Session("t2", RealmId("acme"), "bob"))),
    sessionDb.bind(SessionDb.of(List(Session("t1", RealmId("acme"), "alice"), Session("t2", RealmId("acme"), "bob")))))(
    expect(RealmId("acme"), "t1", Some(Claims(RealmId("acme"), "alice", List("admin", "user"))), "Alice's token at acme: active, with her roles"),
    expect(RealmId("globex"), "t1", None, "acme's token is not good at globex"),
    expect(RealmId("acme"), "t2", None, "Bob was disabled after signing in: his token is no longer active"),
    expect(RealmId("acme"), "t9", None, "no session: signed out, or never issued"),
    reject(RealmId("globex"), "t1", Some(Claims(RealmId("globex"), "alice", List("admin", "user"))), "a token is never good in another realm"),
    reject(RealmId("acme"), "t2", Some(Claims(RealmId("acme"), "bob", List("user"))), "a disabled user's token is never active"),
    reject(RealmId("acme"), "t1", Some(Claims(RealmId("acme"), "alice", List("admin", "user", "owner"))), "roles are never made up"),
    reject(RealmId("acme"), "t1", None, "an active token is not turned away"))
  .keeps(realmIsolation)((realm, token, res) => res match
    case Some(c) => List((realm, c))
    case None    => Nil)
  .expects("A token with no stored session is never active, in any realm")(f =>
    forall((r: RealmId, t: String) => (sessionsByToken(t) == None) ==> (f(r, t) == None)))

OneAtATime.reason: Requests are handled one at a time, so the store after any run is this step applied in turn; induction is the right proof, and it is short. Its witness is the proven code to come.

content.statement: The server starts with distinct tokens, a request keeps tokens distinct, and every request is granted when it may be and changes nothing else.
content.why: The server handles requests one at a time from its initial store, so it is enough that the start has distinct tokens and each step keeps them distinct (by induction over the requests), and that each step does only what was asked. abs: the store after a sequence is the requests applied in turn.

RealmIsolation.reason: One rule for every answer to an application: a new endpoint must keep it or say why it does not apply.

content.statement: No application is ever shown claims of a realm other than its own.
content.why: The idea says a token is only ever good in the realm that issued it. Stated once over every answer the server gives, so a new endpoint (user info, an admin view of sessions) must keep it or say why not.

ReferenceTokens.reason: Sign-out must end a token at once, and a disabled user must lose access: a signed token stays good after both (openIn is only its signature, enabledIn is true). Revisit if applications must check tokens without calling the server.

content.statement: Tokens are random strings that name a stored session; a token is open in a realm when its stored session is of that realm; a user is enabled as their account says.
content.why: A token carries nothing but a reference, so every check reads the session store: a sign-out or a disabled account takes effect at the next check. The cost is a lookup per check, which one server answers from memory.

ServiceWiring.reason: One process with one store, and every request goes through service: a sign-out is seen by the next introspection.

content.statement: Sign-ins, sign-outs and introspections run through service, which checks every result against SignInOut or Introspect, on one in-memory session store.
content.why: Every path to the sessions must go through service; keeping the wiring in one governed file makes a change to it visible. One process holds the store, so a sign-out is seen by the next introspection at once.

SessionTable.reason: Matches the idea: users are found by realm and name, a session opens under a fresh token, and a sign-out only ends its own realm's session.

content.statement: The store is a list of open sessions (token, realm, user); a sign-in opens one for an enabled user whose password hash matches, under a fresh token; a sign-out ends its realm's session of the token.
content.why: A session is what a token stands for, so a session holds its token, realm and user. Users are matched by realm and username: the same name in two realms is two users. A sign-out names its realm, so one realm's application cannot end another realm's sessions.
substitutions: granted := (s: SessionStore, q: AuthRequest, t: SessionStore) => asked(s, q, t)
onlyThat := (s: SessionStore, q: AuthRequest, t: SessionStore) => nothingElse(s, q, t)
vocabulary: users: every realm's users as loaded at start: username, salted password hash, whether enabled, realm roles
uses: case class RealmId(name: String)
case class Session(token: String, realm: RealmId, user: String)
case class SessionStore(open: List[Session])
enum AuthRequest: case SignIn(realm: RealmId, user: String, passwordHash: String, token: String), case SignOut(realm: RealmId, token: String)
case class UserAccount(realm: RealmId, username: String, passwordHash: String, enabled: Boolean, roles: List[String])
distinctTokens = (s: SessionStore) => s.open.forall(a => s.open.forall(b => (a.token == b.token) ==> (a == b)))

asked = (s: SessionStore, q: AuthRequest, t: SessionStore) =>
  q match
    case AuthRequest.SignIn(realm, user, hash, token) =>
      (mayOpen(realm, user, hash) && !s.open.exists(x => x.token == token)) ==> t.open.contains(Session(token, realm, user))
    case AuthRequest.SignOut(realm, token) => !t.open.exists(x => x.token == token && x.realm == realm)

mayOpen = (realm: RealmId, user: String, hash: String) =>
  users.value.exists(a => a.realm == realm && a.username == user && a.passwordHash == hash && a.enabled)

nothingElse = (s: SessionStore, q: AuthRequest, t: SessionStore) =>
  q match
    case AuthRequest.SignIn(realm, user, hash, token) =>
      s.open.forall(x => t.open.contains(x)) &&
        t.open.forall(x => s.open.contains(x) || (x == Session(token, realm, user) && mayOpen(realm, user, hash)))
    case AuthRequest.SignOut(realm, token) =>
      t.open.forall(x => s.open.contains(x)) && s.open.forall(x => t.open.contains(x) || (x.token == token && x.realm == realm))
content.definition:
val sessionTable = oneAtATime.instantiate[(SessionStore, AuthRequest) => SessionStore](
  "SessionTable",
  "The store is a list of open sessions (token, realm, user); a sign-in opens one for an enabled user whose password hash matches, under a fresh token; a sign-out ends its realm's session of the token.",
  why = "A session is what a token stands for, so a session holds its token, realm and user. Users are matched by realm and username: the same name in two realms is two users. A sign-out names its realm, so one realm's application cannot end another realm's sessions."
)(
  Store    := of[SessionStore],
  Request  := of[AuthRequest],
  initial  := SessionStore(Nil),
  distinct := ((s: SessionStore) => distinctTokens(s)),
  granted  := ((s: SessionStore, q: AuthRequest, t: SessionStore) => asked(s, q, t)),
  onlyThat := ((s: SessionStore, q: AuthRequest, t: SessionStore) => nothingElse(s, q, t))
)

Sessions.reason: Both halves of the first section: users can sign in and out, nobody else gets a session; distinct tokens, so a token names one session.

content.statement: In every store the server reaches, tokens are distinct; every sign-in or sign-out is granted when it may be, and changes nothing else.
content.why: The idea's first section, over every sequence of requests: a user can sign in and out (granted), nobody else gets a session (onlyThat), and a token names one session (distinct). What a store, a request and each rule are is left open.

sources.spec:
run => forall((rs: List[Request.T]) => distinct(run(rs))) &&
  forall((rs: List[Request.T], q: Request.T) => onlyThat(run(rs), q, run(rs ++ List(q))) && granted(run(rs), q, run(rs ++ List(q))))

vocabulary: Request: a sign-in or a sign-out sent to the server
Store: the sessions the server keeps open
distinct: whether no two open sessions share a token
granted: whether the second store holds what the request asked for, when it may be granted: a session for a sign-in by an enabled user with their password, the end of the session for a sign-out
onlyThat: whether the change from the first store to the second is only what the request may make: a session opens only for an enabled user with their password, and no other session changes

val sessions = Node.root[List[Request.T] => Store.T](
  "Sessions",
  "In every store the server reaches, tokens are distinct; every sign-in or sign-out is granted when it may be, and changes nothing else.",

content.idea:
# Realms: a small authentication server

Several organisations share one authentication server, like Keycloak. Each
organisation is a realm with its own users. Applications never see passwords:
they send users to the server to sign in, and ask the server whose a token is.

## Signing in and out

A user of a realm can sign in with their username and password. If the user
is enabled and the password is theirs, the server opens a session and gives
back its token, a value no other session has. Anyone else gets no session.

A user can sign out with their token: its session ends at once.

- Token expiry and refresh tokens.
- Which applications may ask (client authentication), consent, and the
  OpenID Connect discovery documents.
- Managing realms and users: they are loaded at start, and an administrator
  can enable or disable a user.

uses: case class RealmId(name: String)
case class Session(token: String, realm: RealmId, user: String)
case class SessionStore(open: List[Session])
enum AuthRequest: case SignIn(realm: RealmId, user: String, passwordHash: String, token: String), case SignOut(realm: RealmId, token: String)
case class UserAccount(realm: RealmId, username: String, passwordHash: String, enabled: Boolean, roles: List[String])
distinctTokens = (s: SessionStore) => s.open.forall(a => s.open.forall(b => (a.token == b.token) ==> (a == b)))

nothingElse = (s: SessionStore, q: AuthRequest, t: SessionStore) =>
  q match
    case AuthRequest.SignIn(realm, user, hash, token) =>
      s.open.forall(x => t.open.contains(x)) &&
        t.open.forall(x => s.open.contains(x) || (x == Session(token, realm, user) && mayOpen(realm, user, hash)))
    case AuthRequest.SignOut(realm, token) =>
      t.open.forall(x => s.open.contains(x)) && s.open.forall(x => t.open.contains(x) || (x.token == token && x.realm == realm))

mayOpen = (realm: RealmId, user: String, hash: String) =>
  users.value.exists(a => a.realm == realm && a.username == user && a.passwordHash == hash && a.enabled)

asked = (s: SessionStore, q: AuthRequest, t: SessionStore) =>
  q match
    case AuthRequest.SignIn(realm, user, hash, token) =>
      (mayOpen(realm, user, hash) && !s.open.exists(x => x.token == token)) ==> t.open.contains(Session(token, realm, user))
    case AuthRequest.SignOut(realm, token) => !t.open.exists(x => x.token == token && x.realm == realm)

val signInOut = sessionTable.contract[SessionStore, AuthRequest, SessionStore](
  "SignInOut",
  "A request keeps tokens distinct, opens a session only for an enabled user with their password, ends only its realm's session of its token, and does what it asks when it may.",
  why = "SessionTable, stated for one request, so each result of the running server is checked. A request that may not be granted leaves the store as it was."
)((s, q, t) => (distinctTokens(s) ==> distinctTokens(t)) && nothingElse(s, q, t) && asked(s, q, t))
  .examples(users.bind(List(UserAccount(RealmId("acme"), "alice", "h-alice", true, List("admin", "user")), UserAccount(RealmId("acme"), "bob", "h-bob", false, List("user")))))(
    expect(SessionStore(Nil), AuthRequest.SignIn(RealmId("acme"), "alice", "h-alice", "t1"), SessionStore(List(Session("t1", RealmId("acme"), "alice"))),
      "Alice signs in to acme with her password: a session under t1"),
    expect(SessionStore(Nil), AuthRequest.SignIn(RealmId("acme"), "bob", "h-bob", "t2"), SessionStore(Nil),
      "Bob is disabled: no session, even with his password"),
    expect(SessionStore(List(Session("t1", RealmId("acme"), "alice"))), AuthRequest.SignOut(RealmId("acme"), "t1"), SessionStore(Nil),
      "Alice signs out: her session ends"),
    reject(SessionStore(Nil), AuthRequest.SignIn(RealmId("acme"), "alice", "wrong", "t1"), SessionStore(List(Session("t1", RealmId("acme"), "alice"))),
      "a wrong password never opens a session"),
    reject(SessionStore(Nil), AuthRequest.SignIn(RealmId("globex"), "alice", "h-alice", "t1"), SessionStore(List(Session("t1", RealmId("globex"), "alice"))),
      "Alice is a user of acme, not of globex"),
    reject(SessionStore(List(Session("t1", RealmId("acme"), "alice"))), AuthRequest.SignOut(RealmId("globex"), "t1"), SessionStore(Nil),
      "globex cannot end acme's session"),
    reject(SessionStore(List(Session("t1", RealmId("acme"), "alice"))), AuthRequest.SignOut(RealmId("acme"), "t1"), SessionStore(List(Session("t1", RealmId("acme"), "alice"))),
      "a sign-out is never ignored"),
    reject(SessionStore(Nil), AuthRequest.SignIn(RealmId("acme"), "alice", "h-alice", "t1"), SessionStore(Nil),
      "Alice with her password is not turned away"))

step = (s: SessionStore, q: AuthRequest) =>
  q match
    case AuthRequest.SignIn(realm, user, hash, token) =>
      if mayOpen(realm, user, hash) && !s.open.exists(x => x.token == token) then SessionStore(s.open ++ List(Session(token, realm, user))) else s
    case AuthRequest.SignOut(realm, token) => SessionStore(s.open.filter(x => !(x.token == token && x.realm == realm)))

SignedTokens.reason: ReferenceTokens was chosen instead: Sign-out must end a token at once, and a disabled user must lose access: a signed token stays good after both (openIn is only its signature, enabledIn is true). Revisit if applications must check tokens without calling the server.

content.statement: Tokens are signed claims (realm, user) an application checks alone: a token is open in its realm while its signature is valid, and its user counts as enabled.
content.why: Like Keycloak's JWT access tokens: an application checks a token with the realm's public key, without asking the server, so a check costs no lookup and works while the server is down. The token carries no session, so the store is never read: openIn is the signature, and enabledIn cannot see the account.

content.statement: A realm's application learns whose a token is exactly when the token's session is open in that realm and its user is enabled there.
content.why: The idea's second section: applications ask whose a token is, and must get the answer when the session is open and the user enabled, and never otherwise. 'Open in that realm' also says a token is only good in the realm that issued it. Sessions, users and realms are left open.

val tokenCheck = Node.root[(Realm.T, Token.T) => Option[User.T]](

  why = "The idea's second section: applications ask whose a token is, and must get the answer when the session is open and the user enabled, and never otherwise. 'Open in that realm' also says a token is only good in the realm that issued it. Sessions, users and realms are left open.",
  idea = "Checking tokens"
)(whose => forall((r: Realm.T, t: Token.T) =>
  whose(r, t).forall(u => openIn(t, r) && holder(t) == Some(u) && enabledIn(r, u)) &&
  (openIn(t, r) ==> holder(t).forall(u => enabledIn(r, u) ==> (whose(r, t) == Some(u))))))

# Realms: a small authentication server

Several organisations share one authentication server, like Keycloak. Each
organisation is a realm with its own users. Applications never see passwords:
they send users to the server to sign in, and ask the server whose a token is.

## Checking tokens

An application of a realm can ask the server whose a token is. The server
answers with the user and their roles in that realm exactly when the token's
session is open in that realm and the user is still enabled; otherwise the
token is not active.

A token is only ever good in the realm that issued it.
